analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes outright.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final weeks of the 107th Congress with zero cosponsors, the bill never left the Ways and Means Committee and received no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have permanently eliminated the federal estate tax (the tax on very large inheritances), along with the gift tax and the tax on generation-skipping transfers. These taxes apply only to estates and gifts above a size threshold, so the benefits of repeal go almost entirely to the heirs of the wealthiest households. The bill was introduced on November 8, 2002, less than two months before the Congress ended, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and died there without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: The heirs of the largest estates. The estate tax in 2002 applied only to estates above a multi-million-dollar exemption, so repeal would deliver its full benefit to the wealthiest few percent of families. It would also spare wealthy families the cost of estate-planning attorneys and trusts, and would benefit anyone planning very large lifetime gifts.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the entire federal estate tax, so heirs of large estates would pay nothing on inheritances that are currently taxed between the 37% and 55% brackets cited in the bill's own findings section.

Also repeals the gift tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax, allowing very large amounts of wealth to be given away during life or passed directly to grandchildren without federal transfer tax.
The repeal would apply to deaths and gifts after December 31, 2002, meaning it would take effect immediately rather than being phased in.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury. The bill's own findings acknowledge these taxes raised about 1% of total federal revenue in fiscal year 1998, roughly $25 billion a year at the time. That revenue would either have to be replaced by other taxes — falling more heavily on people who do pay income and payroll taxes — or made up by more borrowing. The general public would also forgo the modest progressive function the estate tax serves as the only federal tax directly on accumulated wealth at death.

drawbacks.text: Repeal removes roughly 1% of total federal revenue (about $25 billion a year in the late 1990s, per the bill's own findings), which must be replaced by other taxes or borrowing — a cost spread across all taxpayers, while the benefit is concentrated among the largest estates.

Because the tax only applies above a large exemption, the direct benefit goes to a small group of wealthy families; the bill's 'families and small businesses' framing covers a far broader group than those who actually owed the tax.

Supporters counter that the estate tax forces small businesses and farms to liquidate to pay the bill, spawns billions in avoidance costs for accountants and lawyers, and discourages saving — arguments the bill's findings section lays out at length, though the bill provides no analysis of who actually pays the tax.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the small number of families whose estates actually owed the tax, repeal would be worth a great deal. For everyone else, the trade is unambiguous: no direct benefit, and either higher other taxes or more national debt to replace the roughly 1% of federal revenue these taxes raise. The bill is honestly written about the mechanics but not about incidence — it presents repeal as relief for ordinary families and small businesses, while the tax it removes is one of the few that falls almost exclusively on very large accumulated fortunes.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on November 8, 2002 with no cosponsors and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Christopher Cox introduced the Family Heritage Preservation Act on November 8, 2002, a bill to repeal the estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation, and no further action was ever taken.
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: General taxpayers are better off than they would have been under repeal, since the federal government keeps the estate, gift, and transfer taxes and the roughly 1% of revenue they raise. Wealthy estates continue to owe the tax, but Congress had already enacted a separate gradual estate tax phase-down in 2001, so this bill's death changed little for them in the near term.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers, who kept the revenue

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote and drew zero cosponsors from either party, so the record shows no measurable partisan support or opposition beyond the sponsor himself.

industries.note: Full repeal of the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes would eliminate federal tax on the largest inheritances and lifetime gifts, worth tens of billions a year to the top slice of estates. The cost — lost revenue — is spread across all other taxpayers.

industries.industry: Estate-planning attorneys, accountants, and trust services
industries.note: The bill's own findings describe 'legions of tax accountants and lawyers' employed to structure trusts and avoidance devices; outright repeal would eliminate most of that business. Its disappearance would remove a real cost for affected families, but those costs are borne by the same wealthy households who gain the most.

industries.industry: Life insurance companies selling estate-liquidity policies
industries.note: A common use of life insurance is to cover estate tax bills; with no estate tax, that market shrinks. General knowledge about how the product works — the bill text itself does not address this.
